etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English love, luve, from Old English lufu, from Proto-West Germanic *lubu, from Proto-Germanic *lubō, from Proto-Indo-European *lewbʰ- (“love, care, desire”).

The close of a letter sense is presumably a truncation of With love or the like.

The verb is from Middle English loven, luvien, from Old English lufian (“to love”), from Proto-West Germanic *lubōn (“to love”), derived from the noun.

Eclipsed non-native English amour (“love”), borrowed from French amour (“love”).

Cognates include Russian любовь (ljubovʹ), Latin libido (“desire, lust”), Polish lubić and Sanskrit लोभ (lobha, “desire, greed”).

definitions.definition: (uncountable) A deep caring for the existence of another.
A profound and caring affection towards someone.

quote.citation: 1674, John Milton, Paradise Lost:
quote.text: He on his side / Leaning half-raised, with looks of cordial love / Hung over her enamoured.

definitions.definition: Affectionate, benevolent concern or care for other people or beings, and for their well-being.

quote.citation: 1864, Utilitarianism Explained and Exemplified in Moral and Political Government:
quote.text: The love of your neighbor as yourself, is expressly given as the definition and test of Charity,—not alms-giving—and this love is [...] the highest of all the Divine commands[.]

quote.citation: 1963, Martin Luther King, Jr., “A Tough Mind and a Tender Heart”, in Strength to Love‎[1], New York: Pocket Books, published 1964, →OCLC, page 7:
quote.text: Through nonviolent resistance we shall be able to oppose the unjust system and at the same time love the perpetrators of the system. We must work passionately and unrelentingly for full stature as citizens, but may it never be said, my friends, that to gain it we used the inferior methods of falsehood, malice, hate, and violence.

definitions.definition: A feeling of intense attraction towards someone.

quote.citation: 1697, [William] Congreve, The Mourning Bride, a Tragedy. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC, Act III, page 39:
quote.text: Heav'n has no Rage, like Love to Hatred turn'd, / Nor Hell a Fury, like a Woman ſcorn'd.

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter VIII, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC:
quote.text: The humor of my proposition appealed more strongly to Miss Trevor than I had looked for, and from that time forward she became her old self again; for, even after she had conquered her love for the Celebrity, the mortification of having been jilted by him remained.

definitions.definition: A deep or abiding liking for something; an enthusiasm for something.

quote.citation: 2012, Philip Auerswald, The Coming Prosperity, →ISBN:
quote.text: For three decades, the average number of miles driven by US motorists increased steadily. Then, in 2007, that steady climb was suddenly halted. [...] What magic caused Americans to temper their longstanding love of the open road?

definitions.definition: (uncountable) Strong affection.
(countable) A person who is the object of romantic feelings; a darling, a sweetheart, a beloved.

quote.citation: 1595, Edmund Spenser, Epithalamion:
quote.text: Open the temple gates unto my love.

quote.citation: c. 1596–1598 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Merchant of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene ii]:
quote.text: O love, dispatch all business, and be gone!

quote.citation: 1886 October – 1887 January, H[enry] Rider Haggard, She: A History of Adventure, London: Longmans, Green, and Co., published 1887, →OCLC:
quote.text: 'Oh, my love, my love!' she murmured, 'wilt thou ever know how I have loved thee?' and she kissed him on the forehead, and then went and stood in the pathway of the flame of Life.

quote.citation: 1969, The Dubliners, Dirty Old Town:
quote.text: I met my love by the gasworks wall.

definitions.definition: (colloquial, Commonwealth) A term of friendly address, regardless of feelings.
A thing, activity, etc. which is the object of one's deep liking or enthusiasm.

quote.citation: 1997 March, “Faces of Today's Black Woman”, in Ebony, volume 52, number 5, page 96:
quote.text: But it wasn't until [Theresa M. Claiborne] went to ROTC training camp at the University of California at Berkeley that she discovered that flying was her first love. "Pilots talk about getting bit by the flying bug," she says. "I thought, This is heaven."

definitions.definition: (euphemistic) Sexual desire; attachment based on sexual attraction.

quote.citation: 2013, Ronald Long, Men, Homosexuality, and the Gods, Routledge, →ISBN, page 3:
quote.text: The prospect that their cherished Greeks would have countenanced, much less honored, a love between men that expressed itself carnally, however, was not so easily assimilated.

definitions.definition: (euphemistic) Sexual activity.

quote.citation: 1986, Ben Elton et al., “Bells”, in Blackadder II:
quote.text: —What think you, my lord, of... love?—You mean ‘rumpy-pumpy’.

definitions.definition: An instance or episode of being in love; a love affair.

quote.citation: 2014, E. L. Todd, Then Came Absolution, →ISBN:
quote.text: Maybe it was just a summer love, something with no future.

definitions.definition: Used as the closing, before the signature, of a letter, especially between good friends or family members, or by the young.
Alternative letter-case form of Love (“personification of love”).

quote.citation: c. 1810, Samuel Johnson (in The Works of Samuel Johnson):
quote.text: At busy hearts in vain love's arrows fly; [...]

definitions.definition: (obsolete) A thin silk material.

quote.citation: 1664, Robert Boyle, Experiments and Considerations Touching Colours, […] :
quote.text: Such a kind of transparency, as that of a Sive, a piece of Cyprus, or a Love-Hood.

definitions.definition: A climbing plant, Clematis vitalba.
(usually transitive, sometimes intransitive, stative) To have a strong affection for (someone or something).

quote.citation: 1918 September–November, Edgar Rice Burroughs, “The Land That Time Forgot”, in The Blue Book Magazine, Chicago, Ill.: Story-press Corp., →OCLC; republished as chapter VI, in Hugo Gernsback, editor, Amazing Stories, (please specify |part=I to III), New York, N.Y.: Experimenter Publishing, 1927, →OCLC:
quote.text: wanted to take her in my arms and tell her how I loved her, and had taken her hand from the rail and started to draw her toward me when Olson came blundering up on deck with his bedding.

quote.citation: 2013 February 26, Pink, Nate Ruess, Just Give Me a Reason:
quote.text: Just give me a reason, / just a little bit's enough, / just a second we're not broken, just bent / and we can learn to love again.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To need, thrive on.
(transitive) To be strongly inclined towards something; an emphatic form of like.

quote.citation: 1886 October – 1887 January, H[enry] Rider Haggard, She: A History of Adventure, London: Longmans, Green, and Co., published 1887, →OCLC:
quote.text: "I love not that underlings should perceive my wisdom."

definitions.definition: (usually transitive, sometimes intransitive) To seek the good or honor of (someone), care deeply about, to be dedicated to (someone or something).

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, John 3:16:
quote.text: For God so loued þe world, that he gaue his only begotten Sonne: that whosoeuer beleeueth in him, should not perish, but haue euerlasting life.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Matthew 22:37–39:
quote.text: Iesus sayd vnto him, Thou shalt loue the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soule, and with all thy minde. This is the first and great Commandement. And the second is like vnto it, Thou shalt loue thy neighbour as thy selfe.

definitions.definition: (transitive, sometimes ironic) To derive delight from a fact or situation.
(Internet) Synonym of heart (verb).
(transitive, euphemistic) To have sex with (perhaps from make love).

etymologies.etymologyHTML:
Now widely believed (due to historical written record) to be from the idea that when one does a thing “for love” it is for no monetary gain, the word “love” thus implying "nothing".

The former assumption that it had originated from French l’œuf (literally “the egg”), due to its shape, has largely been discredited and is no longer widely accepted. However, the apparent similarity of the shape of an egg to a zero has inspired similar analogies, such as the use of duck (reputed to be short for duck's egg) for a zero score at cricket, and goose egg for "zero".

definitions.definition: (racquet sports, billiards) Zero, no score.

quote.citation: 2013, Paul McNamee, Game Changer: My Tennis Life:
quote.text: The next day Agassi came back from two sets to love down to beat Courier in five sets.

definitions.definition: Nothing; no recompense.

quote.citation: 1916, H. Rider Haggard, The Ivory Child:
quote.text: I fought the white man for less than sixpence. I fought him for love, which is nothing at all.
